findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support requirement jumps to £84m for 2026/27, up 107% from £40.6m actual outturn
findings.detail: 2025/26 required £40.6m emergency government support; the 2026/27 budget shows this rising to £84m—more than doubling in one year. Of eight London authorities using EFS, Haringey is in the second most precarious position. Each £1m of EFS costs approximately £62,000 per year in revenue costs for 20 years at the current 7% interest rate.
findings.matters: The rapid escalation in EFS dependence indicates deteriorating financial control and structural deficit. The 20-year debt servicing cost is material: £84m borrowed at current rates adds £5.2m annually to revenue costs for two decades. This level of EFS dependence is rare among London councils and signals acute financial stress.
findings.figures: £40.6m (2025/26 outturn), £84m (2026/27 budget), £62,000 cost per £1m borrowed per year for 20 years, 7% interest rate
findings.quote: The 2025/26 outturn report showed that the Council required £40.6m of exceptional financial support from government... the 2026/27 budget shows an even greater reliance on EFS, rising to £84 million.

findings.paper_title: CSO 3.1 (vi) Announcements from Cabinet members - External Auditor recommendations under paragraph 2 of schedule 7 of the local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 and the Council's response to those recommendations
findings.headline: Statutory audit recommendation: Council lacks adequate arrangements to identify and deliver savings
findings.detail: KPMG issued a formal statutory recommendation (the most serious audit action) because the Council does not have adequate arrangements to identify and monitor savings schemes. The auditors found specific weaknesses in arrangements for securing value for money, describing it as a risk of significant financial loss. This follows prior years' audit concerns about financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A statutory audit recommendation signals fundamental governance weakness in financial planning and delivery capability. For lenders, this is a material warning that the council may not be able to execute its financial recovery plan.
findings.figures: Recommendation issued 18 May 2026, in response to 2026/27 budget approved 2 March 2026.
findings.quote: Due to the challenging financial position at the Council, and increasing demands on resources, there is a risk that the Council does not have in place adequate arrangements in respect of its identification and monitoring of savings schemes to achieve financial sustainability over the short to medium term. The Council is exposed to a risk of significant financial loss as a result of inadequate arrangements.

findings.headline: Accumulated maintained schools deficit increased to £4.16m; three schools closed with £1.1m deficit charged to council revenue.
findings.detail: The net deficit position on maintained schools deteriorated by £1.53m to £4.16m. Thirty schools are in accumulated deficit (£11.12m) and three schools closed during the year, forcing £1.1m accumulated deficit to be absorbed into council revenue. The council attributes this to falling pupil numbers across the borough but has no long-term strategy to eliminate the deficit.
findings.matters: Deteriorating school finances and closures create one-off revenue charges and signal demographic decline. For lenders, this indicates structural over-capacity and ongoing adjustment pressure that will require service reductions or asset disposal.
findings.figures: Accumulated net deficit £4.16m (increase of £1.53m); 30 schools in deficit (£11.12m); three closures with £1.1m deficit charged to revenue
findings.quote: The accumulated net deficit position on maintained schools increased to £4.16m in 2025/26. This is an increased deficit of £1.53m since last year.

findings.headline: Service-wide overspends (£15.474m) indicate demand is exceeding available funding across multiple services.
findings.detail: Overspends across services totalled £15.474m: Children's £1.903m, Housing Demand £7.041m, Environment & Resident Experience £5.827m. While Adults improved by £6.5m through market management, Children's and Environment remain under pressure. These are labour-intensive or volatile demand services where the council's budgets are insufficient.
findings.matters: Simultaneous overspends across multiple services indicate a systemic issue: either demand is growing faster than forecast, prices are higher than budgeted, or the council is setting budgets below actual need. This pattern suggests future years will face similar or worse pressures.
findings.figures: Children's overspend £1.903m; Housing Demand £7.041m; Environment & Resident Experience £5.827m; total service overspend £15.474m
findings.quote: The overspend against service budgets at outturn is £15.5m. The Adults position improved by £6.5m mainly driven by a smaller than budgeted increase in the price of care placements over the final quarter of the year.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £195.8m (36% underspent) will defer borrowing costs into future years and constrain spending headroom.
findings.detail: The capital programme underspent by £195.8m (36% of budget). Major underspends include Culture/Strategy (£21.7m), Finance & Resources (£20m), and HRA (£120.2m). Most is funded by borrowing. The Corporate Leadership Team is now reviewing options to reduce the programme 'given the current expensive cost of borrowing' (rates above 5%) and considers pausing/stopping schemes. This slippage defers interest costs to future revenue budgets while schemes remain unfinished.
findings.matters: Capital slippage funded by borrowing means interest costs are deferred to future years, worsening medium-term sustainability. Combined with 5%+ borrowing costs, this materially worsens future revenue pressure. For lenders, weak capital forecasting compounds the EFS risk.
findings.figures: £195.8m unspent (36% of £540.4m revised budget); core capital borrowing £93.9m vs £143.3m budgeted; proposed carry forward £55.3m; interest rates above 5%
findings.quote: However, as most of the capital expenditure is funded from borrowing which costs must be budgeted for, there are cost implications for high levels of slippage on general fund revenue budgets.

findings.headline: Housing Demand (temporary accommodation) overspent by £7.041m (23%) with underlying demand remaining uncontained.
findings.detail: Housing Demand budget of £30.956m overspent by £7.041m despite 'Housing Demand programme' interventions (hotel exits, reducing nightly-purchased accommodation). The council supported 2,725 residents in temporary accommodation during the year. While £3.4m was clawed back in-year, the improvement slowed in the final quarter, suggesting interventions are reaching limits. The underlying demand for temporary accommodation remains materially above budget.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is demand-led and volatile. Persistent overspending of this magnitude (23% variance) indicates the council lacks tools to control a major cost driver. For lenders, this suggests demographic/social pressures (homelessness, housing costs) may continue to force deficits regardless of council action.
findings.figures: Budget £30.956m, outturn £37.998m, overspend £7.041m (23%); 2,725 residents in temporary accommodation; Q3 forecast £10.397m, improved only £3.356m to outturn
findings.quote: The actions within the Housing Demand programme drove the reduced spend (-£3.4m) on temporary accommodation including hotel exits and work to reduce both the cost of units and overall reliance on nightly purchased accommodation.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves remain at 'unsustainably low levels' despite General Fund reserve held at only 5% of net budget.
findings.detail: The council maintained the unearmarked General Fund reserve at £15.2m (5% of net budget). The report explicitly describes earmarked reserves as 'unsustainably low'. An unplanned £10.1m was drawn from earmarked reserves in-year to help meet overspends. The HRA reserve was also drawn down to £15.9m, below the £20m target. A forensic review released only £1.4m through reclassification.
findings.matters: Reserves at these levels provide minimal buffer for demographic swings, inflation surprises, or one-off costs. The council's own characterisation of reserves as 'unsustainable' indicates it recognises limited financial flexibility. For lenders, this signals the council is operationally brittle.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve £15.2m (5% of net budget); unplanned drawdown £10.1m from earmarked reserves; HRA reserve £15.9m (below £20m target)
findings.quote: The Council's General Fund reserve has been maintained at £15.2m, however, earmarked reserves remain at unsustainably low levels as set out in Section 9.

findings.headline: £40.5m total debt written off in year-end closedown, with £34.3m aged parking debt from 2021–2024 indicating collection control failure.
findings.detail: The council wrote off £40.5m of debt, predominantly (95%) parking charges. Of this, £34.3m was historical parking debt issued 2021–2024 that became uneconomical to pursue. Bad debt provision for parking increased by £11.2m to £49.8m. A data cleansing exercise revealed years of uncollected debt, suggesting weak arrears management and collection enforcement over a multi-year period.
findings.matters: Large-scale aged debt write-offs indicate poor controls over income collection and arrears management. For lenders, this raises questions about the reliability of budgeted income and whether the council can enforce collection policies to realise projected revenue.
findings.figures: £40.5m total write-offs; £38.5m parking (95%); £34.3m from PCNs 2021–2024; parking bad debt provision £49.8m (increase of £11.2m year-on-year)
findings.quote: Following a data cleansing exercise in Parking, the Council has written off aged debt from previous financial years where it was uneconomical to continue to pursue unrecovered debt. The total write-off comprises of £34.3m historical debt arising from PCNs issued during the financial years 2021–2024.

findings.headline: Agreed savings delivered at only 65%, with auditor issuing Statutory Recommendation on delivery failure.
findings.detail: Of £29.3m agreed savings, only £19.12m (65%) were delivered, leaving a £10.174m shortfall. The report states the council 'has struggled over recent years to deliver agreed savings' and relies on 'fortuitous mitigations' that are 'one-off in nature'. KPMG has issued a Statutory Recommendation specifically addressing this, requiring formal response to Full Council on 20 July 2026.
findings.matters: A sustained inability to deliver agreed savings indicates governance weakness and forecast unreliability. A Statutory Recommendation from external audit is a regulatory escalation signalling serious control deficiency. This directly undermines any financial recovery plan the council proposes.
findings.figures: £19.12m delivered of £29.297m target (65%); £10.174m shortfall; some directorates at 48% (Environment & Resident Experience)
findings.quote: This is one issue that has now been the subject of a Statutory Recommendation from KPMG, the council's appointed external auditor and the Council's response will be presented to Full Council on 20 July.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support requirement of £40.6m exceeds budget by £3.6m, with 2026/27 already planned at £84.3m.
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £37m EFS but now requires £40.6m to balance 2025/26. More concerning, the 2026/27 budget already assumes £84.3m EFS—an increase of £47.3m. The report explicitly states reliance on EFS 'is not a sustainable solution as it creates a revenue pressure from the required borrowing costs being incurred for twenty years'. Over four years (2027/28–2030/31), the cumulative forecast deficit is £239m 'if nothing changes'.
findings.matters: EFS requirements of this scale and accelerating trajectory indicate a structural imbalance in the council's finances that cannot be addressed through one-year actions. Lenders depend on EFS being temporary; here it is growing and becoming permanent debt.
findings.figures: £40.6m required vs £37m budgeted; £84.3m budgeted 2026/27; cumulative deficit £239m 2027/28–2030/31
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget was set with an assumed requirement for £37m exceptional financial support (EFS) from Government. The provisional outturn now presented confirms that £40.6m is required.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan 26 27 v2, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Capital programme delays are masking underlying revenue weakness: Q2 2025/26 shows improved position only because of deferred capital spending.
findings.detail: The council reports a £0.514m Q2 surplus against a budgeted £0.269m. However, it explicitly attributes this improvement to capital programme delays: 'the HRA is still facing huge pressures in repairs and voids and there is a forecast underachievement of income due to high levels of voids. This is mitigated by the forecast reduction in capital financing costs from delays in capital programme schemes.' This means the better headline position masks a deteriorating operational position and depends on continued capital underspend.
findings.matters: When a council's financial position improves only through delaying its capital programme, it signals that the underlying business is stressed. Future programme acceleration will expose the weakness, and deferred investment compounds the maintenance crisis.
findings.figures: 2025/26 budgeted surplus: £0.269m. Q2 revised forecast: £0.514m. Improvement entirely due to 'forecast reduction in capital financing costs from delays in capital programme schemes.'
findings.quote: However, the HRA is still facing huge pressures in repairs and voids and there is a forecast underachievement of income due to high levels of voids. This is mitigated by the forecast reduction in capital financing costs from delays in capital programme schemes.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan 26 27 v2, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Legal disrepair and compensation costs remain an unquantified spending pressure, explicitly flagged as continuing uncertainty.
findings.detail: The statutory finance officer commentary notes that 'costs associated with legal disrepair continues to be a spending pressure and assumptions have been made for costs expected in 2026/27 but this continues to be an area of uncertainty.' No figures are disclosed for the provisions made or the possible range of exposure, making it impossible to assess the adequacy of the budget.
findings.matters: Unquantified legal liabilities that are explicitly flagged as uncertain represent hidden risk to the business plan. If disrepair costs exceed provisions, they will immediately impact an already-stressed revenue position.
findings.figures: Provisions made but figures not disclosed. Flagged as 'continuing to be an area of uncertainty'.
findings.quote: Costs associated with legal disrepair continues to be a spending pressure and assumptions have been made for costs expected in 2026/27 but this continues to be an area of uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan 26 27 v2, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: High void levels cost £2.7m annually and are partly driven by a policy choice the council has identified but chosen not to change.
findings.detail: The budget forecasts void losses of £2.713m in 2026/27. The council identifies that its Neighbourhood Moves Scheme, which allows households with no housing need to access new council homes, incurs 'void costs...without meeting housing need' and notes that 'amending the Neighbourhood Moves Scheme could lead to reduced void costs.' However, no change to this policy is proposed, meaning the council is accepting a quantified cost that it has identified as addressable through policy change.
findings.matters: Void losses represent both lost revenue and wasted building capacity. The fact that management has identified a specific, implementable change that would reduce costs but is not implementing it suggests either political constraints or competing priorities that override financial optimization.
findings.figures: Void loss 2026/27: £2.713m (2.1% of dwelling rent income). Forecast to improve to £1.897m by 2030/31 as new homes deliver.
findings.quote: households who have no housing need are also allowed to move to new homes through the Neighbourhood Moves Scheme. This means that void costs are incurred without meeting housing need. Amending the Neighbourhood Moves Scheme could lead to reduced void costs.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan 26 27 v2, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Responsive repairs costs have spiked to £39.24m following a new policy agreed October 2024, presenting an acknowledged 'significant strain' on the HRA.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 repairs budget is £39.24m, representing a major cost pressure. The council explicitly states this 'presents a significant strain on the HRA' and attributes the rise to 'the new responsive repairs policy agreed by Cabinet in October 2024.' The increase reflects both addressing historic underinvestment and the new commitment to faster repairs. The plan assumes repair costs will decline as capital investment improves the stock condition, but this depends on the capital programme delivering on schedule.
findings.matters: A large, policy-driven increase in operating costs signals either a deferred maintenance crisis or management commitment to new service standards. If repairs costs do not fall as assumed, they will further consume rental income and compress RCCO.
findings.figures: Repairs budget 2026/27: £39.241m (24.6% of total expenditure). Forecast to decline to £33.134m by 2029/30.
findings.quote: The proposed spend on repairs to the housing stock presents a significant strain on the HRA. The increase in spend on repairs shows the Council's commitment to providing a good, timely, repairs service, in line with the new responsive repairs policy agreed by Cabinet in October 2024.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan 26 27 v2, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Interest costs will nearly triple from £31.9m to £94m over ten years, consuming an increasing share of rental income.
findings.detail: Capital financing costs are forecast to grow from £31.92m in 2026/27 (25% of rental income) to £94.007m by 2035/36. The peak pressure occurs in 2030/31 when interest costs consume 46% of dwelling rent income. This reflects accumulation of £1.23bn in new borrowing over the next five years on top of existing debt of £679m. The report notes that every 1% rise in interest rates would add £0.56m to annual costs—a material risk given the debt being accumulated.
findings.matters: A lender must assess debt service sustainability. Interest costs rising to 46% of rental income by 2030/31 leaves minimal headroom for unexpected cost pressures or income shortfalls. This is a highly leveraged position vulnerable to interest rate shocks or income disruption.
findings.figures: Interest costs 2026/27: £31.92m (24.9% of rents). Interest costs 2030/31: £82.62m (46% of rents). Debt Jan 2026: £679m. Forecast borrowing 2026/27-2030/31: £1.232bn. Sensitivity: 1% rate rise = £0.56m.
findings.quote: The cost of capital financing presents a level of challenge and difficulty in delivering the investment needed now and the viability of the HRA in the medium to long-term.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan 26 27 v2, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Revenue contribution to capital has collapsed from an £8m target to £2.62m in 2026/27, with no identified savings to close the gap.
findings.detail: The HRA previously aimed for an £8m minimum annual surplus (RCCO) to reduce dependence on borrowing. The 2026/27 budget achieves only £2.62m, and over the medium term (2026/27-2030/31) totals just £11.85m (averaging £2.37m annually). The council notes it is conducting 'ongoing reviews to identify further efficiencies and savings proposals' but has not yet identified them. This means the £2.09bn capital programme is funded almost entirely through external borrowing rather than self-generated funds.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can generate internal funds to reduce debt burden or is committed to continuously increasing borrowing. The absence of identified savings to close a structural £5m annual gap signals financial strain.
findings.figures: £8m internal RCCO target; 2026/27 actual RCCO: £2.62m; five-year total RCCO: £11.85m
findings.quote: Previously, the plan had an ambition to deliver an £8m minimum annual surplus. This has become increasingly difficult to sustain due to the level of planned investment in existing stock and new build programmes that is required.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - FINAL Capital Strategy 2026-36, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Macroeconomic pressures have made borrowing more expensive and increased cost of essential services
findings.detail: Inflation and economic uncertainty are materially increasing the cost of construction, energy, and care services. Combined with growing demand, these pressures have significantly impacted the Council's financial position and reduced capital investment capacity.
findings.matters: Macroeconomic headwinds are constraining both service delivery and capital investment. If inflation and interest rates remain elevated, the Council's financial position will continue to deteriorate regardless of management action.
findings.figures: Median house prices in borough up 47% since 2014 (£565,000); affordability ratio 14.32 (well above London average)
findings.quote: Inflation and economic uncertainty have significantly impacted the Council's financial position, making borrowing more expensive and increasing the cost of delivering essential services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - FINAL Capital Strategy 2026-36, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Interest rate rise of 1% could render the entire capital programme unaffordable
findings.detail: The Council identifies interest rate volatility as a critical risk. A 1% rise in borrowing costs would push the already heavily borrowed programme beyond affordability limits. The Council relies on long-term fixed-rate borrowing to manage this risk, but exposure remains high.
findings.matters: Interest rate sensitivity at this scale indicates thin margins of affordability. With 75.4% of the programme financed by borrowing, the Council's capital investment is highly vulnerable to rate movements outside its control.
findings.figures: 1% interest rate increase could render programme unaffordable; £715m outstanding borrowing exposure
findings.quote: An increase of 1% could potentially render the programme unaffordable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - FINAL Capital Strategy 2026-36, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Capital programme is being paused or deprioritised for lower-priority schemes to manage affordability
findings.detail: The Council explicitly states it is taking a more focused approach, pausing lower-priority schemes and identifying divestments from underperforming assets. This is a direct response to macroeconomic pressures making borrowing more expensive and reducing programme affordability.
findings.matters: Pausing capital schemes signals financial stress and may indicate the Council cannot deliver previously planned investments in housing, infrastructure, or services. This reduces long-term asset quality and service resilience.
findings.figures: Principle 3 (strategic objectives) represents only 8% of the capital programme (£72.8m of £949.2m)
findings.quote: In response to this, our capital strategy is changing. We are taking a more focused, flexible, and financially sustainable approach, prioritising investments that deliver long-term value and reduce revenue pressures. This includes reviewing the capital programme to reduce borrowing costs, pausing lower-priority schemes, and identifying opportunities to divest from underperforming or financially unsustainable assets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - FINAL Capital Strategy 2026-36, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Forecast overspend of £23m in 2025/26 driven by adult social care and temporary accommodation demand
findings.detail: The Council faces a £23m revenue overspend in 2025/26, primarily from rising demand in adult social care and temporary accommodation. This is after the £37m EFS already secured. The overspend reflects structural service pressures rather than one-off costs.
findings.matters: Recurring service demand overspends signal structural budget weakness. If demand continues to exceed funding, the Council will face repeated deficits, further reliance on capitalisation, and constrained capacity to invest in prevention or efficiency.
findings.figures: £23m forecast overspend 2025/26; £37m EFS secured; driven by adult social care and temporary accommodation
findings.quote: Haringey is under significant financial pressure, with a forecast overspend of around £23 million in 2025/26, primarily driven by rising demand in adult social care and temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - FINAL Capital Strategy 2026-36, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support capitalisation adds £62,000 per year in debt servicing costs per £1m borrowed
findings.detail: The Council secured EFS to balance its budget. Each £1m capitalised in this way adds approximately £62,000 per annum in costs over 20 years. The document states this creates long-term financial pressure by increasing debt servicing, reducing flexibility for future investment, and widening structural gaps in revenue budgets.
findings.matters: EFS is a short-term fix that creates a long-term debt burden. This structural cost increase reduces the Council's capacity to borrow for other purposes and suggests budget deficits will recur unless underlying service costs are addressed.
findings.figures: £1m capitalised = ~£62,000 per year over 20 years; £37m EFS secured for 2025/26 budget
findings.quote: Every £1m capitalised in this way typically adds around £62,000 per year in costs over 20 years, reducing flexibility for future investment and increasing the structural gap in revenue budgets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - FINAL Capital Strategy 2026-36, 10/02/2026 Cabinet , item 12.
findings.headline: Capital programme is 75.4% financed by borrowing with acknowledged need to reduce future increases
findings.detail: The Council is borrowing £715m to finance 75.4% of its £949.2m General Fund capital programme (2026/27-2030/31). The document explicitly states that the next annual review will need to reduce year-on-year borrowing increases and may require re-prioritisation, particularly given reliance on Exceptional Financial Support and high interest rates.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the Council's debt trajectory and capacity. The acknowledged need to reduce borrowing suggests the current programme is unsustainable, and future capital investment will be constrained.
findings.figures: £715m borrowing; 75.4% of programme; £949.2m total General Fund capital budget 2026/27-2030/31
findings.quote: There is a large amount of borrowing being undertaken to pay for the capital programme with 75.4% of the programme using borrowing to deliver schemes and next year's annual review will need to reduce the year on year increase in borrowing for capital investment and may require some re-prioritisation

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Council's historical underfunding recognised but new Fair Funding reform insufficient to close 2026/27 gap
findings.detail: The council notes it received 15% less per resident than neighbouring boroughs and suffered a 55% real-terms cut in core government funding since 2010. Fair Funding reform and a £17.2m increase in 2026/27 are steps forward but leave a £84.3m gap still requiring EFS.
findings.matters: While the council has a structural underfunding argument, the gap remains real and immediate; a lender needs to know that even acknowledged improvements in central funding do not yet solve the council's position.
findings.figures: £143m less in core government funding since 2010 (55% real-terms cut), £17.2m additional funding in 2026/27
findings.quote: By 2024/25 we had £143m less in core government funding, a real-terms 55% cut.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Capital receipts of £5.635m deployed to fund revenue costs and redundancy, reducing capital investment capacity
findings.detail: The council is using capital receipts as revenue support under flexible use rules to help fund its £23.2m savings plan and redundancy costs, rather than investing in assets.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts for revenue reduces future capital investment capacity and asset renewal; this is a short-term fix that defers infrastructure renewal.
findings.figures: £5.635m of capital receipts allocated to revenue/redundancy costs in 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council's planned use for 2026/27 totals £5.635m. This will be targeted at supporting the delivery of the Council's £23.2m of planned savings next year as well as initiatives to  avoid costs.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Financial Recovery Plan now includes independent external governance board
findings.detail: The council is establishing an independent board of sector experts to oversee and hold the council to account for delivery of the Financial Sustainability Plan. This signals recognition of governance or delivery capacity concerns.
findings.matters: External oversight suggests the council or its stakeholders have concerns about execution; it also signals potential changes in how the council is run, which could affect lender confidence or requirements.
findings.figures: Independent board to be established (timing not specified)
findings.quote: Plans are also being put in place to introduce an 'independent board'. This will bring in independent sector experts to oversee and hold the council to account for the delivery of the new Financial Sustainability Plan.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: North London Waste Authority levy rising 7.3% with ongoing Energy Recovery Facility cost uncertainty
findings.detail: The NLWA levy increases to £12.099m (7.3% rise), driven partly by the new Energy Recovery Facility. The report flags that ERF operational start remains uncertain with slippages continuing, generating significant uncertainties about cost forecasts.
findings.matters: External levies are fixed costs the council cannot control; ERF cost overruns would push the levy higher, worsening Haringey's position. Further 11.3% increase forecast for 2027/28.
findings.figures: 7.3% increase to £12.099m (2025/26: £11.274m); 2027/28 levy forecast at c. £13.5m (11.3% increase)
findings.quote: The forecast operational start for the new Energy Recovery Facility ( ERF) continues to remain uncertain with slippages continuing across multiple workstreams. This therefore generates significant uncertainties over how the actual costs will compare to the current forecasts.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Council tax base declining: Band D equivalents down from 82,589 to 80,924
findings.detail: The council's tax base has shrunk by over 1,600 band D equivalents (approximately 2%), while collection rate has also fallen from 95.75% to 92.5%, compounding income pressure.
findings.matters: A declining tax base worsens the structural deficit; fewer residents or lower property valuations mean less revenue even before setting rates, increasing reliance on other funding sources.
findings.figures: 80,924 Band D equivalent dwellings in 2026/27 vs 82,589 in 2025/26; collection rate 92.5% vs 95.75%
findings.quote: The projected income from Council tax in 2026/27 is £145.95m (£141.85m in 2025/26) based on 80,924 Band D equivalent dwellings (the Tax Base) (82,589 in 2025/26), a collection rate of 9 2.5% (95.75% in 2025/26)

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: £8.3m of the £23.2m savings plan comprises new, unproven proposals
findings.detail: Of the council's planned savings, £14.9m were already approved in previous years (existing commitments), but £8.3m are new proposals. The report emphasises focusing relentlessly on achieving all agreed savings, indicating delivery risk.
findings.matters: New savings proposals are unproven; failure to deliver them would worsen the deficit or require deeper cuts or additional EFS requests.
findings.figures: £23.2m total savings (£14.9m approved, £8.3m new)
findings.quote: Our draft budget for 2026/27 includes £23.2m of savings proposals – made up of £14.9m which were approved in previous years and around £8.3 m of new proposals.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: General Fund reserves described as at low levels with £15m minimum floor imposed
findings.detail: The report explicitly states reserves are insufficient and stresses the need to replenish them. The council recommends reserves should not fall below £15m, suggesting current reserves are close to or at this floor.
findings.matters: Low reserves mean the council has minimal buffer for unexpected costs, service volatility, or income shortfalls, increasing financial fragility.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve minimum floor of £15m recommended
findings.quote: These make clear the low levels of reserves currently available to the Council and stress the need to replenish balances over the medium-long term. It is further recommended that the General Fund reserve should not be reduced below £15m.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £323.4m by 2030/31 with no clear closure plan
findings.detail: The five-year medium-term financial strategy shows the gap grows from £84.3m in 2026/27 to £323.4m cumulatively by the end of the period. The council acknowledges the £23.2m annual savings plan is insufficient to close the structural deficit.
findings.matters: This shows the council faces an unsustainable long-term financial position; even with savings, the gap continues to accumulate, indicating structural revenue-raising or service-reduction measures will eventually be needed.
findings.figures: £323.4m cumulative gap by 2030/31, £23.2m savings plan (£14.9m previously approved, £8.3m new)
findings.quote: The outcome of these changes is a forecast budget gap of £84.3m (£37.0m of 2025/26 deficit and £47.3m of 2026/27 deficit) for 2026/27 rising to a cumulative gap of £323.4m by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026/2031 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report
findings.headline: £84.3m Exceptional Financial Support required for second consecutive year to balance budget
findings.detail: The council cannot set a legally balanced budget without this support. The money must be borrowed via Capitalisation Direction or capital receipts, and will incur £10m in financing charges in 2026/27 alone, creating a repayment burden lasting 20 years.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council has a structural deficit it cannot close through revenue alone and depends on annual government permission to borrow to cover day-to-day costs.
findings.figures: £84.3m EFS requirement, £10m financing charges for 2026/27, £37m of 2025/26 deficit carried forward, £47.3m of 2026/27 deficit
findings.quote: Despite this, the Council will still require EFS of £84.3m to set a legally balanced budget in 2026/27. This will be the second year that EFS is required. This is money the council, if agreed will be allowed to borrow , via a Capitalisation Direction or to use capital receipts , to fill its funding gap. It is not a grant and will need to be repaid with financing charges which for the coming year are forecast to cost £10m.

findings.headline: Treasury investment buffer of only £73m against £1,142m total borrowing
findings.detail: As of 31 December 2025, the council held £73.2m in treasury investments while carrying £1,141.9m in borrowing—a ratio of less than 7%. The strategy forecasts treasury investments will remain minimal throughout the forecast period, with a £30m liquidity allowance assumed to cover unexpected cash flow needs within a rolling three-month period.
findings.matters: A limited liquidity buffer significantly restricts the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls without accessing credit markets. This increases financial vulnerability and makes the council dependent on continued access to borrowing facilities at times when credit availability or pricing may be unfavourable.
findings.figures: Treasury investments £73.2m; total borrowing £1,141.9m; target minimum liquidity allowance £30m
findings.quote: On 31 December 2025, the Council held £1,141.9m of borrowing and £73.2m of treasury investments.

findings.headline: £50m LOBO loans face lender option dates from 2027/28 with elevated risk of rate increases
findings.detail: The council holds £50m in LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where lenders can propose interest rate increases at specified option dates starting 2027/28. Given that interest rates remain elevated, the council acknowledges there is "a reasonable possibility that lenders may seek to exercise their options." If rates are increased, the council intends to repay these loans, which would require either accepting higher costs or refinancing at current market rates, typically incurring early redemption premiums.
findings.matters: LOBO loans expose the council to refinancing risk. If lenders exercise their options to increase rates, the council faces either accepting higher ongoing costs or paying a premium to refinance, both of which increase debt servicing costs at a time when the council's financial position is already stressed.
findings.figures: £50m LOBO loans at average rate 4.75%; next option date 2027/28
findings.quote: The Council currently holds £50 million in LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans. The next option date on these loans is not until 2027/28 under which the lender can propose an interest rate increase at specified dates. Given that interest rates remain elevated, there is a reasonable possibility that lenders may seek to exercise their options. If this occurs, the Council intends to repay the LOBO loans to mitigate refinancing risk in future years.

findings.headline: Total capital financing costs forecast to rise 165% from £40m to £106m by 2030/31
findings.detail: Table 12 shows capital financing costs (covering both interest and Minimum Revenue Provision) rising from £40m in 2026/27 to £106m by 2030/31. Interest costs alone are forecast to rise from approximately £20m to £70m across General Fund and EFS combined. This accelerating debt servicing burden will consume an increasing share of the council's revenue budget.
findings.matters: Rapidly escalating debt servicing costs reduce the proportion of revenue available for service delivery and create mounting pressure on the council's financial position. This trend is concerning given the council is already unable to balance its revenue budget.
findings.figures: 2026/27 total financing costs £40m (General Fund £20m interest + EFS £3m interest + £37m MRP); 2030/31 forecast £106m (General Fund £40m + EFS £30m interest + £36m MRP)
findings.quote: There is a revenue impact of the recommended borrowing strategy referred to as Capital Financing Costs, covering both interest costs and the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP).

findings.headline: External borrowing forecast to triple from £981m to £3,024m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council plans to increase external borrowing by up to £2,148m over six years to fund both capital expenditure and EFS capitalisation. This represents a three-fold increase in total external debt, with a single-year borrowing requirement of £621m in 2026/27 alone. The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) grows from £1,419m (actual 31.3.25) to £3,425m (forecast 31.3.31).
findings.matters: A tripling of external debt significantly increases financial risk and locks the council into large long-term debt servicing obligations, reducing future financial flexibility and creating sustained refinancing pressure.
findings.figures: New borrowing requirement up to £2,148m; total external borrowing £981.3m (actual 31.3.25) rising to £3,023.7m (forecast 31.3.31); single-year requirement £621m for 2026/27
findings.quote: anticipated new borrowing requirement of up to £2,148m over the forecast period 2026/27 to 2030/31

findings.headline: Council applying for Exceptional Financial Support from government to balance 2026/27 revenue budget
findings.detail: Haringey has applied to MHCLG for EFS to permit capitalisation of up to £100m of day-to-day running costs in 2026/27. The council explicitly describes its financial position as "challenging" and states this support is required after efforts to reduce costs and identify savings across the medium-term financial strategy have proved insufficient. Notably, the council states this support is not sustainable long-term and work will continue to reduce the EFS requirement in future years.
findings.matters: A requirement for EFS signals that the council's revenue expenditure structurally exceeds its revenue income. This indicates underlying financial stress and makes the council dependent on government support to meet its statutory duty to set a balanced budget.
findings.figures: Up to £100m EFS required for 2026/27; application outcome not known until February 2026
findings.quote: an application to the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for 2026/27 will be required to ensure that in line with statutory duties, a legally balanced budget can be set.

findings.headline: Audit fee for 2024/25 increased to £619,258 including £81,647 in standard variations and £5,081 disclaimed opinion variation; fee variations still being negotiated
findings.detail: Audit scale fee increased from £499,329 (2023/24) to £532,530 (2024/25). Additional standard fee variations of £81,647 cover ISA600r, internal expert work (forensics), VfM risk work, and financial statement additional work. A disclaimed opinion fee variation of £5,081 has been applied. Total fee is £619,258. Fee variations are still being agreed with PSAA and final outcome will be reported later.
findings.matters: Rising audit fees reflect increasing complexity and audit risk at the Council. The disclaimed opinion fee variation suggests KPMG is charging separately for issuing a disclaimer. Unresolved fee negotiations indicate potential further cost escalation.
findings.figures: £619,258 total fee (2024/25); £532,530 scale fee; £81,647 standard variations; £5,081 disclaimed opinion variation
findings.quote: Our scale fee for the 2024/25 audit, as set by PSAA is £532,530 plus VAT (£499,339 in 2023/24). We are in the process of agreeing fee variations with PSAA and will report the final outcome of these at a later date.

findings.headline: Historical housing fraud under forensic investigation; ongoing KPMG analysis of expenditure fraud
findings.detail: Auditors report awareness of historical fraud linked to Housing and are undertaking forensic analysis. This forensic analysis is listed as an outstanding matter that must be finalised before the audit can be signed. While auditors are satisfied the accounts do not contain material risk of misstatement due to fraud, the historical fraud and its scope remain under investigation.
findings.matters: Active forensic investigation of housing-related fraud indicates either the scope is unclear or the fraud is more extensive than initially thought. This raises governance and control environment concerns and suggests possible financial exposure.
findings.figures: Amount of historical fraud not disclosed in auditor sections provided
findings.quote: We are aware of a historical fraud linked to Housing; however, we have reviewed the work undertaken by management and are satisfied that the accounts do not contain a material risk of misstatement due to fraud. Finalisation of KPMG forensics analysis of historical expenditure fraud [is an] outstanding matter

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio generating lost income through overdue rent reviews and lease holdings; £500k recovered to date but large backlog remains
findings.detail: Auditors' risk assessment identified that the Council has not quantified the full extent of income loss from overdue rent reviews and properties with leases on holding over. Management has identified £500,000 in additional income from reviews to date, but explicitly acknowledges a large backlog remains. Additional temporary capacity is being considered to expedite reviews, recognising missed income opportunities are material given the Council's financial position.
findings.matters: Unrecovered commercial property income represents available but unrealised cash flow. The reference to it being 'even more crucial given the Council's financial position' suggests financial pressure and potential cash flow challenges.
findings.figures: £500,000 identified from reviews to date; backlog extent unquantified
findings.quote: Work is underway to work through the portfolio to carry out overdue rent and lease reviews and to date an additional £500,000 has been identified from the reviews to date. However, there remains a large backlog and this will remain a priority until complete. Additional time limited capacity is being considered to expedite these reviews because it is recognised that there are missed income opportunities which are even more crucial given the Council's financial position.

findings.headline: Five significant weaknesses identified in Value for Money arrangements, including 2 on financial sustainability
findings.detail: Audit identified 6 risks of significant weakness in the Council's arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness. These resulted in 5 significant weaknesses: 2 in financial sustainability domain and 3 in improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Value for Money commentary appears in a separate Auditor's Annual Report.
findings.matters: Significant weaknesses in VfM arrangements signal that the Council is not efficiently managing its resources or securing value. For lenders, this indicates governance and operational control concerns that could affect the Council's ability to manage a borrowing programme.
findings.figures: 2 significant weaknesses in financial sustainability; 3 in economy/efficiency/effectiveness
findings.quote: We have identified 6 risks of a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements to secure value for money. Within our Auditor's Annual Report, we have set out our response to those risks.

findings.headline: Journal entry and post-closing adjustment controls remain ineffective for second consecutive year; work to analyse high-risk journals incomplete
findings.detail: Management review controls over journals and post-closing adjustments do not meet auditing standards and remain ineffective from prior year. Auditors planned to analyse all journals through the year using data analytics to focus on high-risk entries, but were unable to complete this work due to delays extracting data from Haringey's ledger and issues mapping the chart of accounts due to large numbers of profit centres.
findings.matters: Ineffective controls over journal entries increase fraud risk and the risk of material misstatement in the accounts. This is a known control weakness that has not been remediated, suggesting limited management action or capability to fix it.
findings.figures: No specific figures; control deficiency noted on prior year
findings.quote: We found the design and implementation of management review controls in relation to journal entries and post-closing adjustments to be ineffective, which is in line with the control deficiency raised in the prior year. We note that this is a common finding in the public sector and is not unique to Haringey, given the large extra resource it would need to implement a control to the level that would meet the requirements of the auditing standards.

findings.headline: Council Dwellings valuation (£1.7bn) cannot be verified; 3 of 60 properties tested had allocation errors or missing evidence
findings.detail: Auditors tested 60 council dwellings to confirm property type and bedroom allocation to valuation beacons. Only 57 of 60 could be confirmed accurate; 2 contained errors and 1 had no supporting evidence. This means the valuation of £1.7bn of assets cannot be relied upon. Additionally, the valuer used national indexation data rather than Haringey-specific data, creating a £18.7m to £16.3m variance.
findings.matters: A £1.7bn asset valuation cannot be verified, creating uncertainty over the Council's true asset base. This is material to the balance sheet and affects borrowing capacity calculations based on asset backing.
findings.figures: £1.7bn (Council Dwellings valuation); 57 of 60 properties verified; £18.7m cautious vs £16.3m optimistic variance on indexation
findings.quote: we tested a sample of 60 properties to agree back to tenancy agreements or fire risk assessments. We were only able to confirm that the property type & number of bedrooms were correct on 57/60 of our sample, and of the remaining 3 items we identified errors in 2 and were unable to obtain any evidence for the final item. As a result, we are not satisfied that the allocation of properties to each Beacon is accurate and cannot conclude our work over Council Dwellings.

findings.headline: Audit opinion disclaimed on 2024/25 financial statements due to inability to obtain sufficient evidence over reserves, asset valuations, and management controls
findings.detail: KPMG has determined there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024, and describes this as pervasive to the Council's financial position. Unable to complete work on Council Dwellings valuation, management override controls, IFRS16, and Housing Revenue Account. A disclaimer of opinion will be issued rather than an audit opinion.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means no independent verification of the financial position. Lenders rely on audited financial statements as a core credit control; this removes that assurance and makes the Council's true financial position uncertain.
findings.figures: £1.7bn (Council Dwellings); £2.9bn total Land & Buildings
findings.quote: there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the Council's and the Group's financial position as at 31 March 2025

findings.headline: Total borrowing requirement of £415m for 2026/27, with Capital Financing Requirement increasing in future years
findings.detail: The council requires £415m in borrowing for 2026/27 to finance the core capital programme and EFS. The council's Capital Financing Requirement is increasing, driven by its capital programme, necessitating additional borrowing in coming years for both General Fund and Housing Revenue Account capital schemes.
findings.matters: Large and growing borrowing combined with unsustainable finances and structural revenue deficit increases debt service obligations and crowds out available revenue for service delivery.
findings.figures: £415m total borrowing requirement for 2026/27
findings.quote: Appendix 1 (Table 2) shows a total borrowing requirement of £415m is required to finance the Council's core capital programme plan and EFS requirement in 2026/27.

findings.headline: EFS support explicitly acknowledged as temporary and unsustainable; council must reach stability by 2027/28
findings.detail: The paper states support through EFS is not a long-term sustainable financial strategy. Work will continue through 2026/27 to reduce EFS drawdown and eliminate any EFS requirement from 2027/28 onwards. This is a time-limited arrangement while the council addresses underlying financial pressures.
findings.matters: The council's own assessment of unsustainability indicates ongoing material risk and need for significant savings or income increases within 12 months to avoid further emergency support.
findings.figures: Target: eliminate EFS requirement by 2027/28
findings.quote: Support through EFS is not a long term sustainable financial strategy and work will continue through 2026/27 to reduce the amount of EFS drawdown and reduce the need for any EFS from 2027/28 onwards.

findings.headline: Council planning to borrow up to £100m to fund day-to-day operational costs rather than capital investment
findings.detail: Under EFS, the government would permit the council to capitalise part of day-to-day running costs by borrowing or using capital receipts to fund operational expenditure. The draft TMSS assumes up to £100m may be required through capitalisation directive for routine services, separate from core capital programme borrowing.
findings.matters: Borrowing to fund operating costs rather than capital investment indicates structural revenue deficit and materially increases credit risk.
findings.figures: Up to £100m may be required through capitalisation directive
findings.quote: For planning purposes, this draft TMSS has been prepared on the basis that up to £100m may be required through a capitalisation directive that allows borrowing for some day to day services will be required.

findings.headline: Council has applied for Exceptional Financial Support due to challenging financial position
findings.detail: Haringey has applied to the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to potentially draw down during 2026/27. The council describes its financial position as challenging despite efforts to reduce costs and identify savings. Outcome will not be confirmed until end of February 2026.
findings.matters: EFS application signals material financial stress requiring government intervention to manage the council's finances, indicating substantial credit risk.
findings.figures: Application outcome due end of February 2026
findings.quote: The Council's financial position is challenging. Efforts to reduce costs and identify additional savings continues but Haringey has made an application to the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to be made available if it is required during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Q1 2025/26 is already forecasting a £30.1m overspend despite the Council's Finance Response & Recovery plan, suggesting the council is off-track again.
findings.detail: Three months into 2025/26, the council is already forecasting £30.1m overspend and only 69% achievement of savings. This mirrors the deterioration pattern of 2024/25 (Q1 £20m → Q2 £37.2m). The budgeted gap for 2025/26 was supposed to be closed by the £29m savings plan, but £14.8m (51%) is already amber or red. KPMG states the Council's approach to financial recovery has 'challenging' targets given prior underperformance.
findings.matters: A lender needs evidence of turnaround. Early Q1 overspend in the financial recovery year shows the same deterioration pattern is repeating and questions whether the recovery plan is credible.
findings.figures: Q1 2025/26 forecast £30.1m overspend; 69% savings achievement forecast; £14.8m of £29m target amber/red (51%)
findings.quote: However, we note as at Q1 2025/26 that the Council is forecasting a £30.1m overspend, as well as an expected achievement of only 69% of its savings target, with £14.8m (over 50% of the target) being amber or red RAG rated.

findings.headline: Haringey's procurement monitoring system identified 924 contracts showing £0 remaining budget but with end dates still to pass, meaning the council cannot reliably detect overspent contracts.
findings.detail: The SAP contract monitoring tool tracks start/end dates and spend vs budget but does not flag overspend or track run rate. Of 924 contracts with £0 remaining, 164 have end dates in 2026 or beyond, implying they are overspent. The council only recently established a Procurement Board (late 2024/25) but remains dependent on manual data collection pending a new e-procurement system. The Procurement Act 2023 (effective 24 Feb 2025) requires publication of a pipeline of contracts ≥£2m within 56 days, but the council is relying on transitional arrangements.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see controls over contract spend. If 924 contracts are opaque to monitoring, the council cannot manage procurement costs or detect overspends until too late.
findings.figures: 924 contracts with £0 remaining budget; 164 with end dates 2026+; first Procurement Board meeting February 2025; PA 2023 effective 24 Feb 2025
findings.quote: For instance, we have reviewed the February 2025 SAP contract monitoring document used by the procurement team and although this provides the start & end dates for contracts across the council, as well as target value & spend to date, it does not track run rate or overspend. We identified 924 instances of a contract showing £0 remaining; however, the contract end date was still to pass – with 164 of these contracts having an end date of 2026 and beyond.

findings.headline: The council has 349 commercial leases 'holding over' on rent and 242 leases with outstanding rent reviews, costing it potentially significant income; one recent review yielded a 21% uplift but the team completed only 8 renewals and 2 reviews in 2024.
findings.detail: The commercial property team has poor data systems and manual record-keeping. 33 properties are vacant (average time empty 1,767 days). The team has no effective system for monitoring repairs, chasing arrears, or forecasting lease income. A 'Property Review' business case has not progressed due to resource constraints. However, 8 lease renewals in 2024 averaged a 21% uplift and 7-year terms, and £500k has been identified from recent reviews. The council does not forecast potential rent increases into budget.
findings.matters: A lender wants to see councils maximise controllable income. Missing £500k+ in near-term income due to poor systems and resource shows poor capital stewardship and leaves money on the table when reserves are depleting.
findings.figures: 349 leases holding over on rent; 242 leases with outstanding rent reviews; 33 vacant properties (1,767 days avg empty); 8 renewals in 2024 (21% uplift avg); £500k identified from reviews; resource for only 8 renewals and 2 reviews in 2024
findings.quote: Additionally, there are 242 leases with an outstanding rent review, meaning that the Council is missing out on a potentially significant amount of income by ensuring that rents are increased in line with market conditions.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation costs spiralled by 19% for nightly paid accommodation and 29% for private sector leases, driving a £9.8m overspend, with 68 families with children illegally in B&Bs for over 6 weeks.
findings.detail: The council spent £35.1m on nightly paid accommodation (NPA), £7.1m on private sector leases (PSLs) and £6.2m on B&Bs/hotels. Household volume increased less than 3% but costs jumped 19-29%. Landlords prefer private rental over PSLs, shrinking the PSL stock by 11% while NPAs rose 4% and B&Bs 41%. The council is breaching the Homelessness Order 2003 (section 17.38) with an average of 68 families with children in B&Bs for over 6 weeks. Haringey lacks sufficient council homes (18-month wait for 1-bed, 12 years for 3-bed).
findings.matters: A lender sees structural cost growth in an area the council cannot control: landlords set rates and supply is constrained. The 12-year wait for permanent housing means TA costs will remain elevated for years.
findings.figures: NPA cost: £35.1m (1,492 households at £824/month avg); 19% cost increase despite <3% volume increase; PSL stock fell 11%; B&Bs/hotels rose 41%; 68 families in B&Bs >6 weeks
findings.quote: The amount of households in TA has increased by less than 3% year on year vs a 19% & 29% increase in the cost of NPAs and PSLs respectively. Additionally, due to the ability of landlords to command significantly higher returns from private rental vs PSLs, the amount of PSLs in place has dropped by 11% and has been offset by a 4% rise in NPAs and a 41% rise in B&Bs/Hotels.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £15.8m in 2024/25 (on top of a built-in £20.4m pressure) and the Care Quality Commission rated the service as 'requires improvement'.
findings.detail: The directorate had a £9.8m overspend forecast by Q1 against a £79m budget. User numbers jumped 14% (from ~1,820 to 2,080 aged 65+, and 1,690 to 1,800 aged 18-64) but were not adequately forecast. The CQC inspection in 2024/25 found people waiting too long for assessment and poor communication. Internal audit identified a £10.7m backlog of outstanding debt (as of June 2024) and 794 clients with no financial assessment completed.
findings.matters: A lender funding a council with uncontrolled adult social care demand faces escalating costs and regulatory risk. The 14% volume jump plus £15.8m overspend shows the pressure is structural, not temporary.
findings.figures: Overspend £15.8m in 2024/25; Q1 forecast £9.8m on £79m budget; user volume increase 14% (aged 65+); £10.7m outstanding debt; 794 unassessed clients
findings.quote: The number of 18–64 year-olds in receipt of a care package jumped from c.1,690 at the outset to 1,740 by Q1 and 1,800 by Q2. This was outstripped by the increases relating to those aged 65+, which rose from c.1,820 users to 1,970 by Q1 and 2,080 by Q2 – a 14% increase.

findings.headline: Haringey is planning continued dependence on government Exceptional Financial Support for 2025/26 (£37m) with a predicted budget gap of over £70m for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council has requested £37m in additional EFS for 2025/26 to balance its budget, on top of the EFS needed for 2024/25. The Fair Funding Review 2.0 modelling shows a potential loss of £30-40m depending on the outcome of the government consultation. Even with a 3.1% increase in government funding settled at spending review, this will be 'outstripped by inflation and not address increasing demand'.
findings.matters: A lender must understand if a council has a plan to become self-sustaining. Continued EFS dependency and an unpredictable £70m+ gap two years out shows structural non-viability without major intervention.
findings.figures: EFS sought for 2025/26: £37m; predicted budget gap for 2026/27: over £70m; Fair Funding Review 2.0 potential loss: £30-40m
findings.quote: Additionally, a further £37 million in EFS has been sought to allow for a balanced budget in 2025/26 and there is currently a predicted budget gap of over £70m for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Haringey achieved only 63% of its 2024/25 savings target (£12.9m of £20.4m), and Q1 2025/26 forecasts only 69% achievement of a much larger £29m target.
findings.detail: By Q2, £10.5m of the £20.2m revised savings target was amber or red RAG-rated, with only £12.9m forecast to be delivered. The final outturn confirms £12.9m delivered. For 2025/26, despite a £29m savings target, Q1 is already forecasting only 69% achievement with £14.8m (over 50%) amber or red. KPMG states: 'we do not believe that the £19.3m efficiency savings planned were sufficiently realistic'.
findings.matters: A lender needs savings to be real and deliverable, not aspirational. Consistently missing targets by one-third shows the council cannot identify or execute the efficiencies it claims, raising doubt about financial recovery plans.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £12.9m achieved of £20.4m target (63%); 2025/26 Q1: 69% forecast of £29m target; £14.8m amber/red rated (51% of target)
findings.quote: The final position for 2024/25 was £12.9m (63%) of savings delivered of the again revised £20.4m target – a £7.5m shortfall.

findings.headline: Haringey's General Fund reserves fell by £45m in a single year, from £97.2m to £52.2m, reducing its financial resilience.
findings.detail: The reduction was driven by a £15.2m drawdown to cover the 2024/25 overspend plus prior year commitments. The council started 2024/25 with already-low reserves (£67.4m at 31 March 2024). KPMG notes the council now has 'particularly low levels of reserves' relative to peers, limiting ability to manage future shocks.
findings.matters: Reserves are a lender's buffer: they show how many months of stress the council can absorb. Depleting them year on year removes that buffer and signals declining financial headroom.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve: £97.2m (31 Mar 2023) → £67.4m (31 Mar 2024) → £52.2m (31 Mar 2025); a £45m fall in one year
findings.quote: The decrease in General Fund Reserve is attributed to the drawdown of £15.2m to cover the General Fund overspend for 2024/25.

findings.headline: Haringey overspent by £37.8m (12.5% of budget) in 2024/25 and required government Exceptional Financial Support to close the accounts.
findings.detail: The council's final outturn was a £37.8m overspend on a £302m General Fund Budget. This was only achieved after drawing down £28m in one-off contributions (contingencies, unallocated reserves, historic credit balances) plus requesting Exceptional Financial Support from the Government. The overspend worsened dramatically through the year: Q1 forecast £20m, Q2 forecast £37.2m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can live within its means. Reliance on government bailouts and one-off reserves draws signals inability to sustain current spending patterns.
findings.figures: £37.8m overspend (12.5% of £302m budget); £28m one-off drawdowns; EFS needed to close accounts
findings.quote: The final year end outturn was a £37.8m overspend which, although an improvement given the trajectory from Q1 and Q2, represents a 12.5% overspend.

news_drafts.headline: External borrowing increased 23.6% in one year; HRA borrowing up 17.6%
news_drafts.lead: A 23.6% year-on-year increase in borrowing raises sustainability questions. When a council describes its own borrowing trajectory as 'not sustainable', it signals expected financial pressure ahead.

news_drafts.headline: PFI and finance lease liabilities breach authorised prudential limit
news_drafts.lead: Exceeding prudential limits in a specific borrowing category reduces headroom and shows the council is operating outside its approved strategy. Persistent breaches may signal deteriorating financial discipline.

news_drafts.headline: £50m LOBO loans face refinancing demand within 12 months at materially higher rates
news_drafts.lead: This is an immediate refinancing obligation. If lenders call, the council faces significantly higher borrowing costs when refinancing at current rates, increasing annual debt service.
